title: A brand kit inside the client portal
metaTitle: A brand kit they can find later
excerpt: Put the logo files, the rules, and the latest version where the client already looks. A zip in an email thread is how the old logo comes back.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The handoff fits a piece about leaving a brand kit where the client can find it.
caption: The current files need a shelf after the meeting. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a brand kit include?
faqs.answer: The logo files you expect people to use, a one-page note that says which file is for which job, the color roles and type jobs, and a date. Add a slide cover or a social image only if someone will actually use it. Leave rejected directions and messy source files out of the folder they open first.

faqs.question: Where should the kit live after delivery?
faqs.answer: In one place the client already uses. On a Hanabi project that place is the client portal, which holds brand files, documents, and updates. The note should say that the portal copy wins if an email attachment disagrees with it. Sending the zip again recreates the problem the portal was meant to solve.

faqs.question: How do you update a kit without creating two versions?
faqs.answer: Replace the file in the portal, date the note, and say in one sentence what changed. Keep the previous set in a folder labeled previous if people might still have a deck open. A silent overwrite, or a new email with no pointer back to the portal, leaves both files looking official.

markdown:
A brand kit delivery is the files, the rules, and the latest version, kept where the client can find them after the presentation is over. A zip in an email thread is how the old logo comes back. Someone saves the attachment, the mark gets a small correction a month later, and the saved zip outlives the correction.

The portal is the shelf. The kit is what you put on it. Both have to be obvious to a person who was not on the kickoff call.

## What belongs in the kit

Keep the kit short enough to scan. The logo files that are actually used: SVG for the web, a transparent PNG, and the version for dark backgrounds. The one-page note that says which file is for which job. The color roles, paper, ink, line, and accent, with their values. The type jobs, if type was part of the work. A date.

Add the things the team will be asked for in the first month, and stop. A social image at the size they post. A simple slide cover that already uses the roles, so the deck does not invent a new blue. An email signature image only if they send one. Each extra item needs a label that says what it is for. Unlabeled extras become the new official version by accident.

Leave the process debris out. Mood boards, rejected directions, and layered source files can live with the studio, or in a clearly named archive the client does not have to open. If a rejected direction sits next to the final mark with a friendlier filename, it will ship on a one-pager. Archive means a folder labeled previous, or no folder at all.

Write the rules as behavior, not as taste. Use the SVG on the site. Use the on-dark files on dark backgrounds. Do not recolor the mark. Do not add a typeface. The sentences should be ones a teammate can follow without you in the room. A paragraph about the feeling of the brand can sit underneath. It cannot be the only instruction.

## One place, and a way to know it is current

Pick the shelf before you export. On a Hanabi project the client portal is that shelf. It already holds brand files, documents, and updates after delivery. The kit goes there, in a section named so a new teammate can guess it: Brand. Inside it, the current files, the one-page note, and the date they were last replaced.

The portal beats a shared drive that has three folders named Brand, Brand Final, and Brand USE THIS. It also beats a chat pin. Pins scroll away. The portal stays on the same URL you already gave them for the project.

Google's page on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks a useful question of any explanation, including a kit: after reading, can someone do the thing they came to do, or will they have to search again? A kit passes when a person can download the logo and apply it without opening a thread from March. If they still search the inbox, the kit is a copy, not the source.

Say, in the note and in the delivery message, that the portal copy wins. "If a file in email disagrees with the portal, the portal is current." That one line retires every attachment you have already sent. Repeat it when you update a file. Updates without that sentence are how two currents exist.

Version in the open. When the accent value changes to meet contrast, replace the page and keep a one-line note of what changed and when. You do not need a heavy version-control lecture. You need a date and a sentence. People can forgive a change they can see. They cannot reconcile two files that both claim to be final.

## Who it is for the week after launch

The founder is one user. The person who makes the next deck, the engineer who puts the logo in the header, and the friend who "just needs the PNG" are the others. The kit has to work for the friend. Names like `logo.png` and `logo-on-dark.png` will. Names like `HB_primary_rgb_v3` will send the friend back to the founder, who will send the old zip.

Write the one-page note in the founder's voice only if that voice is plain. Otherwise write it in the studio's plain voice. Short sentences. The jobs of the files. The colors by role. Where type is used. What not to do. A screenshot of the logo used correctly on paper and on dark.

Access should match the way the company actually works. The founder, the person who edits the site, and the person who builds decks need the kit. A contractor who needs the logo for a one-off can be given the same page, because the page is already safe to share. Do not keep the rules in a private doc and the files in a public link. They will drift.

If the portal has updates, post a short update when the kit changes, in the same place the client already reads project news. "The brand kit has a new accent value. Use the files in Brand. Older attachments are retired." That is an update. A silent replace is a puzzle.

## What the kit is not

It is not a brand book that tries to govern every future poster. A small company will not staff that. Give them the files and the refusals that protect the mark. Leave campaign layouts for the campaigns.

It is not a substitute for the site. The website should already be using these files. If the header and the kit disagree, fix the header before you hand over the kit, or the kit looks theoretical. The first thing a client does is compare the portal to the live site. Make that comparison boring.

It is not a dump of the Figma file with every frame still in it. A Figma link can be part of the kit if they will actually edit there, with a page called Brand that matches the portal, and the other pages left in a working file. Two sources of truth, Figma and the portal, need a sentence about which wins for exported files. Exported files in the portal win for anyone who is not editing the system. The Figma file wins for anyone changing the system with you.

It is not finished when the files are uploaded and nobody has opened them. Sit with the client, or send them a three-step check: open Brand, download the PNG, place it on a dark rectangle using the on-dark file. If they cannot do that from the note, the note is wrong. Fix it while the work is still fresh.

## Keeping it alive without a retainer theater

A kit rots when the product grows and the page does not. New illustration, a dark theme, a second product name. Each of those is either an update to the kit or a decision that the kit does not cover it yet. Write the decision down either way. Silence is how a second logo appears in a mobile app and never makes it back to the portal.

Review the kit when you already have a reason to open the project. A redesign, a new page, a new hire who asks where the logo is. You do not need a quarterly ritual to notice that the social image is two wordmarks old. Fix it when you see it, and date the note.

If the company rebrands, retire the old kit in place. Move it to a previous folder, say the date it stopped, and put the new files in Brand. Deleting the old files overnight strands anyone mid-deck. Keeping them unlabeled strands the new mark. Previous, dated, and visually secondary is the respectful path.

The studio's job at handover is to make the next non-studio edit likely to be correct. That is a smaller job than "own their brand forever," and it is the one that prevents the old logo from returning. Do that job completely. A partial upload, with the rules promised for later, is the zip problem again, only inside a nicer URL.

## A handover you can finish in one sitting

Before you call the kit delivered, use it the way they will.

- The current logo files are in one section, with plain names.
- The note leads with which file to use where.
- Colors and type are the roles, with values, on one page.
- A sentence says the portal wins over email.
- The live site matches the files.
- An update exists if anything changed after the first upload.

Send the link once. Do not also attach the zip "just in case." The attachment is the old habit, and it will win, because downloads are easier than remembering which link was last.

Motion is the next small system that needs the same kind of home. [Motion principles for a small system](/blog/motion-principles-for-a-small-system) is the next piece: two durations and one ease, used to show that something changed, written down so every component does not invent its own personality.

Finished work is easier to judge than a folder of intentions. Browse [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) to see how a small set of decisions holds up on a real page. The kit should be small in the same way.
